title: Capstone: A Verse, Its Contexts and Its Readers
bigQuestion: How can one careful reader describe what a verse says and how others have read it, fairly and with evidence?

story.title: One Ayah, Many Readers
story.kicker: A student spends three weeks with nine Arabic words and finds a thousand years of conversation.
paragraphs: Layla has chosen her verse. It is 2:256, and the first line in Pickthall's 1930 translation is short: "There is no compulsion in religion." She writes it at the top of a clean page. Under it she writes her question: did the commentators read this as a rule for one moment in Medina, or as a principle for everyone? She has three weeks and a stack of library books.

First she lays out two translations. Pickthall has "religion." Rodwell, from 1861, begins "Let there be no compulsion in religion." She notices the difference in tone: one sounds like a fact, the other like a command. She looks up the root of din in Lane's Lexicon and finds religion, obedience, custom and judgment. Suddenly the one short line feels much bigger.

In the second week she reads the commentators, mostly through English summaries. Al-Tabari, writing around 900, gives the story of children raised among the Banu al-Nadir and several views on whom the verse covers. Ibn Kathir, five centuries later, says no one is to be forced into Islam. A modern commentary reads the verse as a charter of freedom of belief. Layla's notes fill with names, dates and arrows.

In the last week she writes. Her thesis names the verse, the readers and the question. One paragraph fairly explains the view that later verses limited 2:256, in the words its holders used. When she presents, a classmate who recites the Qur'an at home and a classmate who never has both nod at the same slide. Nobody asked what Layla believes. They asked how she knew, and she could show them.
story.think: What did Layla gain from reading the verse in two translations and several commentaries instead of one?

sections.title: Choosing a Verse and a Question

lessons.title: Picking Your Ayah
lessons.mainIdea: A strong capstone starts with one short passage and one real question that the passage and its readers can help answer.
reading: Every project in this unit begins the same way: with a single *ayah* (verse) or a very short surah and a question about it. Short is a strength. Surah 103 (Al-'Asr, The Declining Day) has three ayat. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas, Sincerity) has four. A single ayah such as 2:256 or 49:13 can fill an essay. A student who picks all of Surah 2, with its 286 ayat, will only skim.

The question matters as much as the verse. A weak question asks for a fact: "What surah is 2:256 in?" A strong question asks what the words mean and how readers have taken them: "Does 2:256, 'There is no compulsion in religion,' describe a rule for rulers, a fact about belief, or both, and how have commentators decided?" A strong question has more than one serious answer. That is what makes it a *research question*.

Choose a passage you can study fairly. The goal is to describe what the text says and how Muslims and scholars have read it, not to prove the Qur'an true or false. A good test is this: could a Muslim classmate and a non-Muslim classmate both read your finished essay and say it described the text and its readers accurately? If yes, the question is a good one for a public school.

words.d: a verse of the Qur'an; the word also means sign; plural ayat
an open question with more than one serious answer, which evidence from texts and readers can help settle
how much a project tries to cover; a narrow scope lets a writer go deep

look.title: Three Starting Questions
look.text: Student A: "What does the Qur'an say about everything?" Student B: "What surah number is Al-Ikhlas?" Student C: "Surah 49, ayah 13 says people were made into nations and tribes 'that ye may know one another.' How have classical and modern commentators read the purpose of human difference in this verse?"
look.prompt: Which student has a workable capstone question? What is wrong with the other two, and how would you fix one of them?

check.q: Why does the unit advise choosing a single ayah or a very short surah?
choices: Long surahs may not be quoted in a public school
A short passage lets the writer study its words, context and readers in depth
Only short surahs have commentaries written on them
Short surahs are the only ones that are Meccan
check.why: Scope: a narrow passage can be read closely with its contexts and commentators; a long surah can only be skimmed.

check.q: Which of these is a research question rather than a fact question?
choices: How many ayat are in Surah 112?
Which surah is called The Cow?
In what year did Pickthall publish his translation?
How have commentators read the purpose of human difference in 49:13?
check.why: A research question has more than one serious answer; the others have one factual answer.

check.q: What is the fairness test the lesson suggests for a capstone essay?
choices: Readers of different faiths could agree it describes the text and its readers accurately
The essay proves which reading of the verse is true
The essay avoids quoting the Qur'an at all
The essay uses only modern translations
check.why: The course studies what the text says and how it is read, without asserting or denying its truth.

lessons.title: Two Translations Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Reading a verse in two English translations shows where translators made choices, and those choices point to questions worth asking.
reading: Every English Qur'an is a translation, and Muslims widely hold that a translation is an interpretation of the meaning, not the Qur'an itself. That is why Pickthall called his 1930 book The Meaning of the Glorious Koran. For the capstone, you read your verse in at least two translations, and at least one must be public domain so you can quote it exactly. Pickthall (1930) is this course's text. J. M. Rodwell (1861), E. H. Palmer (1880) and George Sale (1734) are older public-domain choices.

Put the two versions next to each other and mark every place they differ. Sometimes the difference is only old or new English: "thee" and "you." Sometimes it is a real choice. One translator may add words in brackets to explain; another may leave the Arabic spare. One may render a word as "religion," another as "faith" or "way of life." Each difference is a clue about what the Arabic allows.

Modern translations such as Yusuf Ali (1934), Arberry (1955), Muhammad Asad (1980) and The Study Quran (2015) are still under copyright. You may describe how they render a phrase, and you may paraphrase their notes, but you do not quote them at length. Cite every translation by translator and year, so a reader can check your work.

words.d: a rendering of a text in another language; many Muslims call a Qur'an translation an interpretation of its meaning
free of copyright, so it may be quoted and copied; Pickthall's 1930 translation entered it in the United States in 2026
the particular words a translator chooses for a phrase

look.title: Pickthall on 2:256
look.text: There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:256 (Al-Baqarah), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Find this ayah in a second translation. List every word that differs, and say which difference changes the meaning and which is only style.

check.q: Why did Pickthall title his book The Meaning of the Glorious Koran?
choices: He did not know Arabic and worked from a French version
The title was required by his publisher's copyright
He held, as many Muslims do, that a translation conveys the meaning but is not the Qur'an itself
He translated only the meanings of the Meccan surahs
check.why: Many Muslims hold that only the Arabic is the Qur'an; a translation renders its meaning.

check.q: Which translation may you quote exactly and at length in the capstone?
choices: Arberry (1955)
The Study Quran (2015)
J. M. Rodwell (1861)
Muhammad Asad (1980)
check.why: Rodwell is public domain; the other three are still under copyright and may only be described or paraphrased.

check.q: A student notices that one translator writes "religion" and another "faith" for the same word. What should she do?
choices: Treat it as a clue about what the Arabic word allows and look into it
Pick the one she likes and ignore the other
Decide that one translator made an error
Stop using translations and quote only the Arabic
check.why: Differences between translations point to real choices in rendering the Arabic, which are worth studying.

lessons.title: Words and Their Roots
lessons.mainIdea: Most Arabic words grow from a three-letter root, so looking up the root of a key word shows the range of meanings a translator had to choose from.
reading: Arabic builds most words from a *root* of three consonants. The root k-t-b carries the idea of writing: kitab (book), katib (writer), maktab (office or school). The root s-l-m carries the idea of wholeness and peace: salam (peace), islam (submission or surrender to God), muslim (one who submits). When a translator meets a word in an ayah, the root shows its family of meanings.

Take the key word of 2:256, din, rendered "religion" by Pickthall. Classical dictionaries list a range for it: religion, obedience, custom, and judgment or requital, as in yawm al-din, the Day of Judgment, in 1:4. The word translated "compulsion," ikrah, comes from a root about dislike and forcing someone against their will. Knowing that range helps a student see why commentators could read the ayah in more than one way.

You do not need to read Arabic to do this well. Edward William Lane's Arabic-English Lexicon (1863–1893) is public domain and lists roots with their classical meanings and examples. Many online Qur'an tools also show each word's root. Record the root, the range of meanings, and which meaning each of your translators chose. Say plainly that you are working from a lexicon, not from your own reading of the Arabic.

words.d: the set of consonants, usually three, from which a family of related Arabic words is built
an Arabic word rendered religion, way of life, obedience or judgment, depending on the verse
a dictionary, especially one that gives a word's older meanings with examples
compulsion; forcing someone to do what they dislike, the word used in 2:256

look.title: One Root, Many Words
look.text: s-l-m: salam (peace), salim (whole, sound), islam (submission to God), muslim (one who submits). d-y-n: din (religion; judgment), dayn (a debt), yawm al-din (the Day of Judgment, 1:4). A translator reading din in 2:256 had to choose which part of this family fits.
look.prompt: Why might a commentator connect the ideas of religion, debt and judgment? How could knowing the root change how you read 2:256?

check.q: What does an Arabic root usually consist of?
choices: A single vowel sound at the start of a word
A whole ayah that other ayat repeat
A prefix that marks a word as a verb
Three consonants that carry a core idea
check.why: Most Arabic words grow from a three-consonant root, such as k-t-b for writing.

check.q: Which word shares the root s-l-m with islam?
choices: kitab
salam
din
ikrah
check.why: Salam (peace) and islam (submission) both come from s-l-m; kitab is k-t-b, din is d-y-n.

check.q: How should a student who does not read Arabic use a lexicon in the capstone?
choices: Claim to have translated the verse personally
Record the root and its range of meanings, and say the work comes from a lexicon
Ignore roots and rely on one translation only
Choose the rarest meaning to make the essay original
check.why: Honest citation means naming the lexicon as the source of the word study.

lessons.title: The Surah Around the Verse
lessons.mainIdea: An ayah sits inside a surah with its own shape, setting and themes, so reading the verses around it is the first step in reading it well.
reading: A verse read alone can mislead. Scholars call the verses around it the *siyaq*, the context in the text. Ayah 2:256 comes right after 2:255, the Throne Verse, which describes God's knowledge and power over all things. Right after it, 2:257 contrasts those who follow God into light with those led into darkness. Many readers see 2:256 as a hinge: after describing God's greatness, the passage says belief cannot be forced.

Next, place the surah. Standard Egyptian editions of the Qur'an, printed from 1924 on, label each surah Meccan or Medinan, following Muslim tradition about when it was revealed. Most counts give 86 Meccan and 28 Medinan surahs, though scholars differ on a few. Al-Baqarah is Medinan, from the years the early Muslim community lived as a small city society after the hijra of 622. Short Meccan surahs like 103 and 112 tend to focus on God's oneness, the Last Day and right action.

Then sketch the surah's shape. Some modern scholars, among them Neal Robinson and Raymond Farrin, argue that long surahs such as Al-Baqarah are built in a ring, with matching parts around a center. Others read the surahs as linked blocks of themes. You do not need to settle that debate. Just show where your ayah sits and what comes before and after it.

words.d: the context of a verse within the text: the verses before and after it
labels for surahs based on Muslim tradition about whether they came before or after the hijra of 622
a structure some scholars see in surahs, with matching sections arranged around a center

look.title: Meccan and Medinan Surahs
look.cite: Standard Cairo edition of the Qur'an (1924) labels; counts vary slightly among scholars
look.prompt: About what share of surahs is labeled Meccan? Why might a Medinan surah deal with community life more than a short Meccan one?

check.q: What is siyaq?
choices: The occasion of revelation reported in hadith
The rules for reciting an ayah aloud
A commentary written by al-Tabari
The verses before and after an ayah, its context in the text
check.why: Siyaq is textual context; the occasion is asbab al-nuzul, and recitation rules are tajwid.

check.q: Which verse comes just before 2:256?
choices: 2:255, the Throne Verse, about God's knowledge and power
1:1, the opening of Al-Fatihah
112:1, the opening of Al-Ikhlas
9:5, a verse about fighting
check.why: Ayah 2:255, Ayat al-Kursi, directly precedes 2:256 in Surah Al-Baqarah.

check.q: On what are the Meccan and Medinan labels based?
choices: Whether the surah names the city of Mecca or Medina
The length of the surah in the Cairo edition
Muslim tradition about whether a surah came before or after the hijra of 622
Which city's scholars wrote the first commentary
check.why: The labels follow tradition about timing relative to the hijra, not place names in the text.

lessons.title: The Occasion of Revelation
lessons.mainIdea: Reports called asbab al-nuzul tell when and why some verses were revealed, and commentators use them, carefully, to read a verse.
reading: Muslim scholars gathered reports about the moments that prompted particular verses. These are the *asbab al-nuzul*, the occasions of revelation. Al-Wahidi of Nishapur (died 1075) wrote a well-known book of them. Not every verse has one, and for some verses the reports disagree. Scholars also debated whether a verse applies only to its occasion or to everyone. A common principle holds that the general wording counts, not the particular cause.

For 2:256, al-Tabari (died 923) records several reports. The best known, also found in the hadith collection of Abu Dawud, tells of women in Medina whose children had not survived. They vowed that if a child lived, they would raise it among the Jews. When the Jewish tribe of Banu al-Nadir was expelled from Medina, some of those children were among them. Their Muslim relatives said, "We will not leave our sons," and the verse is reported to have come then. The children were not forced.

Historians handle these reports with care. They were written down generations later, and more than one occasion is often given for the same verse. So a strong essay says "al-Tabari reports" or "according to al-Wahidi," not "this is what happened." Treat the occasion as one context among several, alongside the words, the surah and the long history of reading.

words.d: the occasions of revelation: reports about the events that prompted particular verses
scholar of Nishapur (died 1075) who compiled a well-known book of the occasions of revelation
Persian-born scholar in Baghdad (died 923) whose large commentary gathers earlier reports on each verse

look.title: An Occasion for 2:256
look.text: Al-Tabari reports that some women of Medina vowed to raise their children among the Jews if the children lived. When the Banu al-Nadir left Medina, those children were with them, and their families wanted to bring them back. The verse on no compulsion is reported to have come then, and the children were left free to choose.
look.cite: Al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan (commentary), on 2:256, c. 900s; the report is also in Sunan Abu Dawud; paraphrased
look.prompt: If this occasion is right, who was being told not to use force, and on whom? Does the general wording reach beyond this case?

check.q: What are asbab al-nuzul?
choices: The seven accepted readings of the Qur'an
Rules for dividing the Qur'an into thirty parts
Reports about the events that prompted particular verses
Names given to the 114 surahs
check.why: Asbab al-nuzul means the occasions of revelation, compiled by scholars such as al-Wahidi.

check.q: According to the report al-Tabari records, what prompted 2:256?
choices: Muslim families wanting to keep children raised among the Banu al-Nadir
A debate between Muhammad and Christian visitors from Najran
The conquest of Mecca in 630
A question about fasting in Ramadan
check.why: The best-known report ties 2:256 to children raised among the Banu al-Nadir, who were not forced.

check.q: Why does a careful essay write "al-Tabari reports" instead of stating the occasion as fact?
choices: Al-Tabari was not a Muslim scholar
The Qur'an forbids discussing occasions
All occasion reports have been proved false
The reports were written later and sometimes give more than one occasion
check.why: Historians note that occasion reports were recorded later and can conflict, so they are attributed.

lessons.title: The Qur'an Explaining Itself
lessons.mainIdea: Classical scholars held that the best explanation of one verse is another verse, so a capstone traces the key words of its ayah across the whole book.
reading: A common principle of *tafsir* (commentary) holds that the Qur'an explains itself. Ibn Taymiyya (died 1328) wrote that the best method is to explain the Qur'an by the Qur'an, then by the Prophet's sayings, then by the words of his Companions. Scholars call this tafsir al-Qur'an bi'l-Qur'an. In practice it means finding other verses that use the same word or treat the same theme.

For 2:256 a student might gather 10:99, where God asks the Prophet whether he would compel people to believe, and 18:29, which says the truth is from your Lord, so let whoever will believe and whoever will disbelieve. A student might also read 9:5 and 9:29, verses about fighting. Some classical scholars held that those later verses limited or abrogated 2:256. Others, like Ibn Kathir (died 1373), read 2:256 as a lasting principle that no one is forced to enter Islam.

Laying verses side by side is how the commentators themselves worked. It is also where their disagreements come from. When you trace your key word through the Qur'an, record every verse you use with surah name and number. Then report which scholars connected which verses, and what each concluded.

words.d: commentary on the Qur'an that explains its words, context and meaning
explaining the Qur'an by the Qur'an: reading one verse in the light of others
naskh; the view held by many classical scholars that a later verse can replace the rule of an earlier one
Syrian scholar (died 1373) whose widely read commentary explains verses by other verses and hadith

look.title: Three Verses on Belief and Choice
look.text: 2:256 says there is no compulsion in religion. 10:99 asks the Prophet whether he would compel people until they believe. 18:29 says the truth is from the Lord, so whoever will may believe and whoever will may disbelieve. (All three paraphrased from Pickthall, 1930.)
look.prompt: What idea do the three verses share? Why might a commentator who reads them together find it hard to call 2:256 abrogated?

check.q: What does tafsir al-Qur'an bi'l-Qur'an mean?
choices: Reciting the Qur'an with its full tajwid rules
Explaining a verse by other verses of the Qur'an
Translating the Qur'an into Persian
Copying the Qur'an in Kufic script
check.why: It names the method of reading one verse through others, praised by Ibn Taymiyya among others.

check.q: How did some classical scholars and Ibn Kathir differ about 2:256?
choices: Some held it was Meccan; Ibn Kathir held it was Medinan
Some held later verses limited or abrogated it; Ibn Kathir read it as a lasting principle
Some rejected it from the text; Ibn Kathir accepted it
Some read it about fasting; Ibn Kathir read it about prayer
check.why: The disagreement is over abrogation and scope, not over whether the verse belongs to the Qur'an.

check.q: Which verse fits best with 2:256 in a study of belief and choice?
choices: 2:255, the Throne Verse on God's power
112:1, say He is Allah, the One
96:1, read in the name of thy Lord
18:29, whoever will may believe and whoever will may disbelieve
check.why: 18:29 treats the same theme of freely chosen belief; the others treat different themes.

lessons.title: The Classical Commentaries
lessons.mainIdea: A handful of classical commentaries, Sunni and Shia, are the standard places to see how a verse has been read over a thousand years.
reading: Long before modern scholarship, Muslim scholars wrote verse-by-verse commentaries. Al-Tabari (died 923) gathered the reports of earlier generations and often weighed them. Al-Zamakhshari (died 1144) focused on grammar and style. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (died 1210) wrote a vast commentary full of philosophy and theology. Al-Qurtubi (died 1273) drew out legal rulings. Ibn Kathir (died 1373) explained verses by other verses and by hadith.

Shia scholars wrote major commentaries too. Al-Tusi (died 1067) and al-Tabrisi (died 1153) wrote classical works. In the 20th century, Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i (died 1981) wrote al-Mizan, which reads the Qur'an by the Qur'an. Sufi commentators such as al-Qushayri (died 1072) looked for inner, spiritual meanings. A strong capstone uses at least two classical voices and, where it fits, notes Sunni, Shia or Sufi readings without ranking them.

Most of these works are in Arabic, but parts of several are in English, and The Study Quran (2015) summarizes many of them in its notes. When you use a summary, say so: "according to The Study Quran's note on al-Razi." Your job is to report what each commentator said and why, in your own words, with the name and the verse.

words.d: a scholar who writes tafsir, explaining the Qur'an verse by verse
Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (died 1210), author of a large commentary rich in theology and philosophy
a 20th-century Shia commentary by Muhammad Husayn Tabataba'i that reads verses in the light of other verses
tafsir that seeks inner, spiritual meanings in the text alongside its outer sense

look.title: When the Commentators Died
look.cite: Standard reference works, e.g. Encyclopaedia of Islam; dates rounded to the year
look.prompt: How many centuries separate al-Tabari and Tabataba'i? What might each have known that the other did not?

check.q: Which commentator is best known for focusing on grammar and style?
choices: al-Zamakhshari
al-Qurtubi
Tabataba'i
al-Qushayri
check.why: Al-Zamakhshari's commentary centers on language; al-Qurtubi on law, Tabataba'i on verse by verse, al-Qushayri on Sufi meanings.

check.q: Al-Mizan is a commentary from which tradition and century?
choices: Sunni, 10th century
Sufi, 11th century
Shia, 20th century
Sunni, 14th century
check.why: Tabataba'i, a Shia scholar who died in 1981, wrote al-Mizan.

check.q: A student reads about al-Razi only in The Study Quran's notes. How should she cite it?
choices: Al-Razi wrote, followed by a long quotation she made up
The Qur'an means, with no source named
According to The Study Quran's note, al-Razi reads the verse this way
All Muslims agree, with no commentator named
check.why: Honest citation names the summary used and attributes the reading to the commentator.

lessons.title: A Modern Reader
lessons.mainIdea: Modern commentators read the Qur'an with new questions, and adding one modern voice shows how an old verse speaks to a new age.
reading: Readers in the last two centuries brought new questions to the text. Muhammad Abduh (died 1905) of Egypt urged fresh reasoning and taught a commentary later completed by his student Rashid Rida. Sayyid Qutb (died 1966) wrote In the Shade of the Qur'an, a political and spiritual commentary. Muhammad Asad (died 1992) added full notes to his translation, The Message of the Qur'an (1980). Fazlur Rahman (died 1988), who taught at the University of Chicago, argued for reading verses by the moral aims behind them.

Modern readers often disagree with each other as much as with the classical scholars. On 2:256, many modern writers read the ayah as a charter of religious freedom for all people. Others stay closer to the classical debate on who it covers. Some women scholars, such as amina wadud in Qur'an and Woman (1992), reread verses on gender by looking at the Qur'an's wider principles.

For the capstone, choose one modern reader who actually wrote about your verse or its theme. Describe the reading in your own words, since modern works are under copyright. Then place it beside your classical voices. Does the modern reader agree, build on them or break from them? Say which, and give the reason the modern reader offers.

words.d: tafsir written since the 1800s, often addressing new questions of society, science and rights
Pakistani-born scholar (died 1988) at the University of Chicago who read verses through the moral aims behind them
translator and commentator (died 1992) whose The Message of the Qur'an (1980) adds extensive notes

look.title: Old and New Side by Side
look.text: A classical commentator explains 2:256 by asking whom the rule covered in Medina and whether later verses changed it. A modern commentator explains it by asking what it means for citizens of many faiths living under one law. Both begin from the same Arabic words.
look.prompt: What different questions are the two readers asking? Can both readings be accurate descriptions of what the verse has meant?

check.q: Which modern scholar taught at the University of Chicago and read verses by their moral aims?
choices: Fazlur Rahman
Sayyid Qutb
Rashid Rida
al-Tabari
check.why: Fazlur Rahman taught at Chicago; Qutb wrote in Egypt; Rida completed Abduh's commentary; al-Tabari is classical.

check.q: Why should a student paraphrase rather than quote Muhammad Asad at length?
choices: He wrote only in Arabic
His work is not a commentary
Public schools may not mention modern scholars
His 1980 work is still under copyright
check.why: Modern translations and commentaries are under copyright; describe or paraphrase them.

check.q: What does the lesson say modern readers often do?
choices: Repeat al-Tabari word for word
Disagree with each other as much as with the classical scholars
Reject the Arabic text for a translation
Agree on one reading of every verse
check.why: Modern commentary is varied; readers bring different questions and reach different conclusions.

lessons.title: Acknowledging Other Readings
lessons.mainIdea: A fair essay names the readings it does not follow and explains them accurately, which makes its own argument stronger.
reading: Every serious reader of a verse knows other readers disagree. Classical commentators often listed several views and then said which they preferred. Al-Tabari regularly wrote that people of interpretation differed and gave each view. A capstone should do the same. This part of an essay is sometimes called the *counterargument*, but here it is not about winning. It is about describing the whole conversation.

Describe the other reading at its best, in words its holders would accept. If you argue that 2:256 is read by most modern commentators as a general principle, say plainly that many classical scholars held it was limited or abrogated, and give their reason: they read it together with later verses on fighting. Then explain why others disagreed. Do not call a reading ignorant or extreme without showing where scholars answered it.

One more kind of difference matters. Muslims read the Qur'an as the word of God. Many historians and scholars of religion study it as a text in history. Your essay does not choose between those views. It can report both: how believers have read a verse, and what historians say about its setting. That is what describing the text fairly means.

words.d: a reading or view that differs from the one the writer argues, described fairly in the essay
describing another view at its strongest, in terms its holders would accept
naming who holds a view or reads a verse a certain way, instead of stating it as simple fact

look.title: A Verse on Human Difference
look.text: God addresses humankind: people were created from a male and a female and made into nations and tribes so that they might come to know one another, and the most honored of them before God is the most righteous.
look.cite: Qur'an 49:13 (Al-Hujurat), after the translation of Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930; paraphrased
look.prompt: One reader says this verse is about lineage and pride; another says it is about how nations should treat each other. How would you present both fairly?

check.q: What did al-Tabari often do before giving his own view?
choices: Ignore any view he disagreed with
List the differing views of earlier interpreters
Quote only Persian poets
Refuse to say which view he preferred
check.why: Al-Tabari gathered and presented competing interpretations, then often weighed them.

check.q: What is a charitable reading of another view?
choices: Agreeing with it to be polite
Leaving it out so the essay stays short
Calling it a mistake without a reason
Describing it at its strongest, in words its holders would accept
check.why: Charitable reading means presenting a view fairly and fully before responding to it.

check.q: How does the capstone handle the difference between believers and historians?
choices: It reports both views without choosing between them
It decides that historians are correct
It decides that believers are correct
It leaves both views out of the essay
check.why: The course describes how Muslims read the Qur'an and what historians say, without ruling on truth.

lessons.title: Writing a Thesis
lessons.mainIdea: A thesis for the capstone makes a claim about what the verse says and how it has been read, and every part of it can be checked against sources.
reading: A *thesis* is the one-sentence claim your whole essay supports. In this course, a thesis is not about whether the Qur'an is true. It is about the text and its readers. Here is an example: "Classical commentators such as al-Tabari tied 2:256 to a specific moment in Medina and debated its reach, while many modern readers treat it as a general principle of religious freedom; both readings build on the verse's context in Surah 2."

Look at what makes it work. It names the verse. It names readers. It makes a claim someone could dispute, since another student might argue the classical and modern readings are closer than this. And every part can be checked: a reader can open al-Tabari, a modern commentary and Surah 2 and see whether the thesis holds.

Build the essay from the thesis. A useful order is: the verse in two translations; its place in the surah; its occasion, if reports exist; two classical readings; one modern reading; other readings you do not follow; and your conclusion. Each paragraph should begin by saying which of these it covers.

words.d: the single central claim an essay argues and supports with evidence
the passages, commentaries and facts that support a claim, each one cited
a statement that can be supported or disputed with evidence

look.title: Which Thesis Works?
look.text: Thesis 1: "The Qur'an is a beautiful book." Thesis 2: "Surah 103 is short." Thesis 3: "In 103:3, commentators read 'exhort one another to truth' as a duty shared by the community, and modern readers have applied it to public life, showing how a three-ayah Meccan surah became a guide for groups, not only for individuals."
look.prompt: Which thesis can be argued and checked with sources? What is missing from the other two?

check.q: What does a capstone thesis in this course make a claim about?
choices: Whether the Qur'an is revealed by God
Which religion is the most accurate
What a verse says and how it has been read
Which translation is holy
check.why: The course studies the text and its readers and does not rule on religious truth.

check.q: Why is "Surah 103 is short" a weak thesis?
choices: It is false, since Surah 103 is long
It quotes a copyrighted translation
It is a fact no one would dispute, so there is nothing to argue
It names too many commentators
check.why: A thesis must be a claim that could be disputed and supported with evidence.

check.q: In the suggested essay order, what comes right after the verse in two translations?
choices: Its place in the surah
The student's conclusion
The modern reading
Readings the essay does not follow
check.why: The suggested order moves from translations to the surah, the occasion, classical and modern readings, others, and conclusion.

lessons.title: Citing, Presenting and the Rubric
lessons.mainIdea: Clear citations, a short presentation and a shared rubric let others check your work and see how it will be judged.
reading: Cite the Qur'an by surah name and number and by ayah: Al-Baqarah 2:256. Name the translator and year every time you quote: Pickthall, 1930. Cite commentators by name, work and verse: al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan, on 2:256. If you used a summary, name it. Hadith are cited by collection, such as Sahih al-Bukhari or Sunan Abu Dawud. Put your sources in a list at the end.

The capstone also has a short *presentation*, about five minutes. Show the verse in two translations on one slide. Show where it sits in the surah. Then give the two or three readings and your thesis. If you play a recording of the ayah recited, say so beforehand, and keep it short. Listeners should leave knowing what the verse says and how people have read it.

A rubric tells you how the work will be judged before you start. The one below gives the most weight to accurate description of the text and its readers, and to fair treatment of readings you do not follow. Clear writing and correct citations count too. Nothing on the rubric asks what you believe.

words.d: a note naming exactly where a quotation or idea came from: surah and ayah, translator, commentator, year
a short spoken report that shares the verse, its readings and the thesis with the class
a scoring guide that lists what the work will be judged on and how much each part counts

look.title: Capstone Rubric Weights
look.cite: Course rubric for this capstone, Architecture of Grace
look.prompt: Which two parts carry the most weight? Why might a course on studying a sacred text weigh them that way?

check.q: Which is a complete citation for a quoted verse?
choices: The Qur'an, somewhere in the middle
Surah 2, from memory
A website about Islam
Al-Baqarah 2:256, trans. Pickthall, 1930
check.why: A full citation gives surah name and number, ayah, translator and year.

check.q: How should a student cite a hadith?
choices: By the surah and ayah where it appears
By the collection, such as Sunan Abu Dawud
By the page number of Pickthall
By the reciter who recorded it
check.why: Hadith are not in the Qur'an; they are cited by the collection that preserves them.

check.q: What does the rubric not ask about?
choices: Fair treatment of other readings
What the student personally believes
Accurate translations
Correct citations
check.why: The rubric judges accuracy, context, commentators, fairness and citation, not belief.

lessons.title: Studying Scripture in a Public School
lessons.mainIdea: U.S. public schools may teach about religion, including a sacred text, when the teaching is academic and does not promote or reject any faith.
reading: In 1963 the U.S. Supreme Court decided Abington School District v. Schempp. It ruled that public schools may not lead students in devotional Bible reading or prayer. In the same decision, the Court said schools may teach about religion. Justice Tom Clark wrote that the Bible may be studied for its literary and historical qualities when presented objectively as part of a secular program of education.

That is the line this whole course has walked. You have learned what the Qur'an says, how it was written down and recited, and how Sunni, Shia, Sufi and modern readers have understood it. You have not been asked to believe or disbelieve. Many Muslim students recite the Qur'an at home or at a mosque; many classmates have never opened it. An academic course gives both a shared way to talk about it.

Take a moment to reflect. What did you learn from reading one verse so closely? What surprised you about how many ways careful people have read it? How did it feel to describe a view you do not hold in words its holders would accept? Those skills reach well beyond the Qur'an. They help with any text people care deeply about, and with any neighbor who reads it differently.

words.d: 1963 Supreme Court case that ended school-led devotional Bible reading but allowed teaching about religion
learning what religions teach and practice and how they have been read, without promoting or rejecting them
done as an act of worship, such as prayer or reading scripture for faith

look.title: The Court on Studying Religion
look.text: It might well be said that one's education is not complete without a study of comparative religion or the history of religion and its relationship to the advancement of civilization.
look.cite: Justice Tom C. Clark, majority opinion, Abington School District v. Schempp, 374 U.S. 203 (1963)
look.prompt: What does Justice Clark think a complete education includes? How does this course fit his description?

check.q: What did Abington v. Schempp (1963) rule?
choices: Schools may not mention religion at all
Schools must teach one religion's scripture
Schools must lead a daily prayer
Schools may not lead devotional Bible reading, but may teach about religion
check.why: The Court ended school-led devotional reading while affirming academic study of religion.

check.q: Which activity fits the academic study of religion?
choices: Comparing how two commentators read 2:256
A teacher asking students to accept the Qur'an as true
A teacher telling students the Qur'an is false
A class leading a prayer before the lesson
check.why: Academic study describes texts and readings; it does not promote or reject a faith.

check.q: According to the lesson, what skill from the capstone reaches beyond the Qur'an?
choices: Memorizing the whole of Surah 2
Choosing the one correct religion
Describing a view you do not hold in words its holders would accept
Reciting with full tajwid rules
check.why: Fair, charitable description helps with any text people care about and any neighbor who reads it differently.

review.q: What makes a good capstone question?
choices: It has one factual answer
It asks whether the Qur'an is true
It is open, with more than one serious answer that sources can help settle
It covers the whole Qur'an at once
review.why: A research question invites evidence from the text and its readers.

review.q: Which pair are both public-domain English translations?
choices: Pickthall (1930) and Rodwell (1861)
Arberry (1955) and Asad (1980)
Yusuf Ali (1934) and The Study Quran (2015)
Pickthall (1930) and Arberry (1955)
review.why: Pickthall, Rodwell, Palmer and Sale are public domain; the others are under copyright.

review.q: A student studies the verses right before and after 2:256. What is she studying?
choices: The asbab al-nuzul
The tajwid
The qira'at
The siyaq, its context in the text

review.q: Which scholar compiled a well-known book on the occasions of revelation?
choices: al-Zamakhshari
al-Wahidi
Tabataba'i
Fazlur Rahman
review.why: Al-Wahidi of Nishapur (died 1075) wrote on asbab al-nuzul.

review.q: Why did some classical scholars hold that 2:256 was limited or abrogated?
choices: They believed it was not part of the Qur'an
They read it together with later verses on fighting
They thought it was a Meccan verse
They found it only in Rodwell's translation
review.why: The abrogation debate linked 2:256 with later verses such as 9:5 and 9:29.

review.q: Which commentator is Shia and wrote in the 20th century?
choices: al-Tabari
Ibn Kathir
al-Qurtubi
Tabataba'i
review.why: Tabataba'i (died 1981) wrote al-Mizan; the others are classical Sunni scholars.

review.q: Which thesis fits the course's approach?
choices: Classical and modern readers read 2:256 differently, and both build on its context
The Qur'an is the only true scripture
The Qur'an was not revealed
Everyone reads 2:256 the same way
review.why: A course thesis makes a checkable claim about the text and its readers, not about truth.

review.q: What did Justice Clark say in Abington v. Schempp?
choices: Religion may never be mentioned in school
Schools should hold daily prayer
Education is not complete without studying the history of religion
Only the Bible may be studied in school
review.why: Clark affirmed objective, academic study of religion while ending devotional exercises.
